blocks.h2: Where Is the Water Coming From?

tiles.body: If water rises through the floor drain, the sewer is pushing back. That's a backup, not a leak.

tiles.h3: Mortar Joints in an Old Foundation
tiles.body: In historic homes, groundwater seeps through stone and brick joints during long wet spells.
A downspout that empties next to the house sends roof water straight to the foundation.
Water from a supply line, washer hose or water heater. Shut off the water first.

blocks.intro: In September 2008, about 9 inches of rain fell on Geneva over two days, and basement flooding was reported around town. Older and newer homes flood for different reasons.

items.body: Homes near the river built in the 1800s have foundations that were never meant to be waterproof. Interior drain tile and a sump pit are often the most practical fix.
Some historic basements still have no sump pit. Adding one gives groundwater somewhere to go besides across the floor.

items.h3: Floor Drains Tied to the Sewer
items.body: Older floor drains connect straight to the sewer. In a big storm, that's where water comes up. A backflow valve or [overhead sewer](/geneva/overhead-sewer-systems) stops it.

items.h3: Finished Lower Levels in Newer Homes
items.body: Newer homes often have finished basements, so a failed [sump pump](/geneva/sump-pumps) or a missing battery backup does more damage.

bodies: Waterproofing keeps groundwater out of the basement. Our part is the plumbing behind it: sump pits and pumps, battery backups, discharge lines and the drain tile that carries water to the pit.

In older Geneva homes, adding a sump pit and interior drain tile is often the most effective fix for walls that seep. We check the system and tell you what will actually stop the water. For water coming up through drains, see [sewage backup service](/geneva/sewage-line-backup-services).

blocks.h2: Basement Flooding Questions From Geneva Homeowners

items.q: My basement floods but I don't have a sump pump. What are my options?
items.preview: Adding a pit and pump, often with interior drain tile.
items.answer: In many older Geneva homes, we can cut a sump pit into the floor and connect interior drain tile to it. The pump then sends groundwater outside before it reaches the floor.

items.preview: Clear water at the walls is groundwater. Dirty water at the drain is sewage.
items.answer: Clear water seeping in at walls or along the floor edge is groundwater. Dirty, smelly water rising from the floor drain or a basement fixture is sewage backing up.

items.q: What should I do right now?
items.preview: Stay safe, stop the source if you can and call.
items.answer: Keep away from water near outlets or appliances. If a pipe or appliance is leaking, close the main. If the floor drain is backing up, stop using water. Then call us.
Yes. We install, repair and replace backflow valves that keep sewer water from coming up through basement drains.

items.q: What does basement flood repair cost in Geneva?
items.preview: It depends on the source and the fix. You'll approve a flat price first.
items.answer: It depends on where the water is coming from and what it takes to stop it. You'll approve a flat-rate price for each option before we start.
